title: The lamb
hookLine: a child asks a lamb who made it, and answers: he who calls himself a Lamb (The Lamb)
tomorrow: where does God live? Blake points at a human face.

cards: Bedtime, bath time, the back seat of the car: that's where the big questions land. Why is the sky blue? Where did Grandpa go?
Who made me? Blake wrote a poem where a child takes that kind of question to a lamb in a field: "Little Lamb who made thee / Dost thou know who made thee".
It's a soft, singsong poem, easy to learn by ear, and its question is a very big one. The lamb, of course, can't answer. So the child does.

teach.b: Here's the answer: "Little Lamb I'll tell thee, / Little Lamb I'll tell thee! / He is called by thy name, / For he calls himself a Lamb: / He is meek & he is mild, / He became a little child". The answer is Christ.
Blake leans on John's Gospel, where John the Baptist sees Jesus coming and says: "Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world." And the child sees the knot that ties them together.
The lamb is named for him; he became a child; so the child and the lamb share his name: "I a child & thou a lamb, / We are called by his name."

That's the Christian teaching under the poem, the incarnation: God came close in a gentle form, as a child, and is called the Lamb. It's why at Mass Catholics sing the Agnus Dei, Lamb of God, before communion.
Now set it beside yesterday. The Tyger asked whether the Lamb's maker made the tiger, and left it open. The Lamb answers in a child's voice, simply and sure.

teach.h: TWO CONTRARY STATES OF THE SOUL.
teach.b: Blake's title page calls these songs "Shewing the Two Contrary States of the Human Soul."
In Blake's pairing, innocence isn't foolish and experience isn't wrong. The child's answer and the grown-up's question both belong to the soul, and he printed them side by side.

how: At Mass, Catholics sing or say the Agnus Dei, Lamb of God, before communion, and the priest repeats John the Baptist's words; Blake's The Lamb is sung as a carol and a children's song in some churches and schools.

games.q: at Mass with a friend, you hear everyone sing Lamb of God. afterward she asks why Jesus is called a lamb. what fits today?
o: John the Baptist called him the Lamb of God, and Blake's child says he became a child too.
Jesus worked as a shepherd as a boy, so people named him after his sheep.
it's a nickname from Blake's poem that the churches later borrowed.
games.why: the name comes from John 1:29, long before Blake. Blake's child adds the knot: he is meek and mild, he became a little child, and we are called by his name.

practice: For two minutes, look at something gentle near you: a sleeping pet, a child's drawing, a soft blanket, a plant's new leaf. Let your face soften as you look.
If you pray, you can say the poem's last line over it: Little Lamb God bless thee.
